Mainstream estimates commonly use the idea of **excess mortality**: compare expected deaths (based on pre-famine trends) to actual deaths during 1959–61/62.

Low-casualty arguments often object that:
- the “baseline” death rate was chosen too low (making the excess artificially high);
- normal mortality in 1950s rural China was already high and volatile, so the “expected” deaths are uncertain;
- some of the apparent loss is due to undercounting births (a “birth deficit”) rather than deaths.

They may claim that analysts mistakenly convert missing births into deaths, or that big parts of the demographic “gap” reflect fewer births and delayed registrations.
